subsystems.name: Sensing layer
subsystems.role: detects both the structure's own state and the biological needs of occupants — temperature, humidity, CO₂, light, sound, occupancy, contact.
parts: embedded fibre-optic strain and temperature sensors
capacitive or pressure sensing in floors and walls
biosignal sensors (heart rate, skin temperature) for occupants who opt in

subsystems.name: Living tissue layer
subsystems.role: engineered cells or plant tissue grown in place, able to grow, heal and respond to stimuli.
parts: genetically engineered bacterial or mammalian cells
hydrogel or cellulose scaffold holding the cells

subsystems.name: Vascular supply network
subsystems.role: keeps the living tissue fed and removes waste, the way blood vessels serve an organ.
parts: microfluidic channels moulded into the structure

subsystems.name: Structural skeleton
subsystems.role: carries loads while housing the channels, sensors and actuators.

subsystems.name: Actuation layer
subsystems.role: physically rearranges the structure — opening, thickening, shifting or reconfiguring.
parts: turgor-driven plant cells or swellable gels

subsystems.name: Control layer
subsystems.role: turns sensor data into movement, deciding when the structure should respond and when to stay still.

subsystems.name: Containment and life-support envelope
subsystems.role: protects the living material from weather, contamination and desiccation, and keeps it in.

buildSteps.title: Define what the structure must sense and do
buildSteps.detail: Start from the biological needs to be served — air quality, thermal comfort, light, space — and set measurable targets rather than aiming at 'sentience' in general.

buildSteps.title: Engineer the living material
buildSteps.detail: Synthetic-biology methods write gene circuits into cells so they respond to chosen cues: glowing, contracting, secreting, or repairing a crack. Work happens in contained labs with killed-cell controls.

buildSteps.title: Design the vascular network
buildSteps.detail: Channels of tens to hundreds of micrometres are laid out so no living cell is more than a short distance from nutrients and oxygen, mirroring how real tissue is perfused.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the skeleton
buildSteps.detail: Carbon-nanotube composite members are laid up or printed, with the fluid channels, sensor fibres and actuator pockets cast in during manufacture rather than drilled afterwards.

buildSteps.title: Seed and grow the tissue
buildSteps.detail: The living layer is inoculated into its scaffold under sterile conditions and grown to a working thickness over days to weeks in a controlled facility.

buildSteps.title: Integrate sensing and actuation
buildSteps.detail: Fibre-optic and chemical sensors are connected to the control layer, and actuators are calibrated against the range of movement the skeleton can safely allow.

buildSteps.title: Close the control loop
buildSteps.detail: Controllers are trained on simulated and short real trials so that sensor readings produce proportionate movement, with hard limits that prevent self-damage.

buildSteps.title: Commission, then maintain
buildSteps.detail: The module is installed, monitored for tissue health and structural strain, and given a maintenance cycle of feeding, weeding out contamination and replacing worn living components.

prerequisites.why: bacteria and plant cells have been grown inside concrete, hydrogels and textiles, but only as small or short-lived components.
nanotube fibres with exceptional strength exist at laboratory and small industrial scale; a load-bearing building skeleton is not available.
soft robots and shape-morphing panels work at furniture scale, not at the scale of rooms that must also carry loads.
buildings already adjust heating and lighting to occupancy, but not the physical form of the structure.

prerequisites.tech: Long-term viability of living tissue in building envelopes
prerequisites.why: keeping engineered tissue alive for years through heat, frost and drought is the central unsolved problem.

pathway.milestone: self-healing concrete, algae bioreactor façades and fibre-optic sensing built into bridges
pathway.unlocks: a first generation of structures that react to their condition, not to people.

pathway.milestone: modular living panels that heal cracks or change their shading and insulation in response to weather
pathway.unlocks: living materials as replaceable building components rather than whole buildings.

pathway.milestone: perfused living skins supplied by a building-wide nutrient network, with closed-loop control
pathway.unlocks: rooms whose surfaces respond to occupants' air quality, comfort and use.

pathway.milestone: structures that sense, feed and reshape themselves, with carbon-nanotube skeletons carrying the loads
pathway.unlocks: buildings that adapt and repair without human intervention — if tissue life-support and biosafety can be made routine.
